positioning: An American cowboy with a mysterious Australian name.
story: The Australian Shepherd is not from Australia. It is as American as a rodeo, and it was born on Western ranches.
The name came from Basque shepherds who reached the American West by way of Australia in the 1800s. Ranchers saw their dogs work, and the name stuck. So did the dogs.

They were bred to herd sheep and cattle across big country. They needed brains, stamina, and an eye for the whole flock. The breed has all three, plus a coat in four colors and eyes that sometimes do not match.
Rodeos made the Aussie a star in the 1950s and 1960s. Trick dogs jumped, balanced, and stole the show. The AKC recognized the breed in 1991.
Today Aussies guide the blind, search for the lost, and visit the sick. At home, they herd children, cats, and the vacuum cleaner. An Aussie with no job will invent one.
Give it a task, a field, and a family to keep track of. It will watch over all of it, and it will watch you most.
rank_cap: A cowboy’s dog with a mistaken name (AKC)
fblocks: Basque shepherds reached America by way of Australia. Ranchers called their dogs Australian Shepherds. The name outlasted the story.
Jay Sisler’s rodeo dogs, who dazzled crowds with tricks in the 1950s and 1960s. Aussies also work as guide and search dogs.
Brilliant and busy, so a bored Aussie herds the family. Breeders avoid pairing two merles, which risks deafness and blindness.
A medium double coat in blue merle, red merle, black, or red. Eyes may be blue, brown, amber, or one of each.
Forty to sixty-five pounds. Developed in the American West. Recognized by the AKC in 1991.
days: Independence Day. Old Tex sleeps through the parade. He has seen enough of them.
Not Australian at all. The Aussie was built on American ranches.
Fireworks light the valley. Dusty watches every burst. He counts the flock anyway.
Aussie eyes can be blue, brown, amber, or one of each. Both work fine.
A pink nose and a good slice of watermelon. That is a complete summer.
Aussies love to catch things. A water balloon never stood a chance.
Puppies on a flag quilt. One asleep on Tex’s paw. He will not move it.
last_walk:
The smoke drifts, and the dirt road glows pink.
Dusty and Sage walk home after the fireworks. Her ears still twitch at every echo. He walks a step ahead and checks back. It is an old habit. A herder counts heads, and tonight all heads are home.
